## Animations

The animation below shows the **secant parabola** (degree-2 Newton polynomial through $x_0 - h$, $x_0$, $x_0 + h$) converging to the **tangent parabola** (degree-2 Taylor polynomial at $x_0$) as $h \to 0$, for $f(x) = \sin(x)$ centered at $x_0 = 1$, the running example of Mathews' module; the frames include its Figure 1 and Figure 2 step sizes $h = 0.1$ and $h = 0.01$.

Julia source scripts that generated these animations are linked under each case.

The module's Examples 3–5, which extend the construction to Newton polynomials of higher degree through equally spaced points starting at $x_0$ and compare them with the Taylor polynomial of the same degree (the tangent cubic in Examples 3 and 4, a higher-degree tangent polynomial in Example 5), are not animated here.

### Case 1 — Secant parabola $\to$ tangent parabola as $h \to 0$, $f(x) = \sin(x)$, $x_0 = 1$

**Behavior:** For large $h$ the secant parabola is determined by three well-separated points. As $h \to 0$ all three nodes collapse to $x_0$, and the secant parabola approaches the Taylor polynomial $T_2(x) = f(x_0) + f'(x_0)(x-x_0) + \tfrac{1}{2}f''(x_0)(x-x_0)^2$ — the tangent parabola. This shows that the Taylor polynomial is the limiting position of the Newton interpolating parabola.

[Julia source](tangparabaa.jl)

![Secant parabola (red dashed) through three nodes converging to the tangent parabola (green dotted, Taylor degree-2) as h shrinks from 1.0 to 0.01, followed by the tangent parabola alone, for sin(x) at x0=1](tangparabaa.gif)
